queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the dozens of small knobbly regrowth points ringing its base, scars from repeated pollarding over the decades. It stands on the corner of Wilhelminakade and Oranjesingel.
queue.story:
The organisation this tree was planted for was not yet fifty years old when it got its own tree, whatever the sign says. Groningen planted a line of lindens along the Wilhelminakade in 1928 to honour the ANWB, then still a cyclists' union rather than the roadside-assistance name it later became, and the register calls it the union's fiftieth anniversary. The ANWB itself dates its founding to 1883, which makes 1928 the forty fifth year, not the fiftieth. Nobody has explained the gap, and this page will not invent one.

queue.name: The ANWB Linden of Wilhelminakade

queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the leaves, narrower and more textured than an ordinary sessile oak's, and by the drooping tips of its broad loose crown. It stands on the east edge of the Noorderplantsoen, in sight of Werfstraat.
queue.story:
Most oaks in Noorderplantsoen are the ordinary native kind, but this one carries a cultivar name, Mespilifolia, medlar-leaved, for foliage that reads narrower and more textured than a typical sessile oak's. It grows on the park's eastern edge, clearly visible from the residential street the park backs onto, which is exactly why the Dutch national monumental tree register singles it out from the small group it was registered alongside as the specimen worth calling monumental.

queue.name: The Mespilifolia Oak of Noorderplantsoen
queue.worth: closes a gap: this tree has no photograph at all

queue.recognise: You can recognise it by its thinning crown but intact trunk base, standing alone at the centre of the square. It stands in Martinikerkhof, in the shadow of the Martini Tower.
queue.story: For decades in the twentieth century, Groningen parked cars on top of this oak's roots. Martinikerkhof, one of the city's three great squares, spent the years up to the 1970s as a parking lot before the city cleared the cars and let it become what it is today, a quiet, largely car-free green space in the shadow of the Martini Tower. The oak stood through all of it, in the middle of the square, and the municipality's own 2021 survey rates its condition as moderate to poor, noting plainly that the tree appears to be declining in recent years even though the ground around it is now far better than the parking lot it endured for decades. queue.tree_name: The Green Beeches of the Nieuwe Kerkhof
queue.recognise: You can recognise the pair by their scars, one in front of the Nieuwe Kerk with a long-healed wound, the other beside the church with a woodpecker-hollowed break and a self-seeded oak at its foot. They stand on the church lawn.
queue.story:
A parked lawn beside a seventeenth century church holds one of Groningen's largest stands of old beeches, roughly thirty of them by some counts, and the Dutch national monumental tree register singles out two as genuinely exceptional. One stands in front of the Nieuwe Kerk with a long-healed wound in its trunk; the other, beside the church, carries an old broken-limb scar that woodpeckers have since hollowed out and that a self-seeded oak has taken root beside.

queue.recognise: A vast hollow yew with a split red-brown bole and many stems beside the porch of St Mary's church, one heavy limb propped on concrete stilts.
queue.story:
The Friends of Linton Yews say this tree could be up to 1,500 years old and a strong contender for the oldest tree in England. Its girth is over 9 metres, and the Ancient Tree Forum notes that it is certainly well past the 800 years at which a yew counts as ancient. A reader who sent it to us gave the same 1,500. Nobody can date it exactly, because the heart has rotted away and there are no rings to count.

It stands hard by the porch of St Mary's church, which is twelfth century with Anglo-Saxon roots, and the yew may be older than the building. The Friends add that its girth has not changed since it was measured in the early 1800s.

queue.note:

queue.tree_name: The Monterey Cypress over the Creek
queue.recognise: A big Monterey cypress with a fluted, buttressed trunk and long horizontal limbs reaching out over a tidal creek, a bench beside it.
queue.story:
A reader walking a path above a tidal creek near Carne, on the Lizard side of the Helford River, called this "a spectacular tree hanging over the creek" and added that there is a lovely bench to sit and ponder. Both halves of that are easy to believe.

The trunk flares into deep, fluted buttresses at the base and rises in long vertical ridges of grey-brown bark. Several heavy limbs run out horizontally over the water, and a few of them end in old pruning cuts where the tree has been kept clear of the path. Above them the crown is dense and dark green.
